H1: the confirmatory test is inconclusive, due to trustworthiness failing to meet reliability criterion.

Theoretical implications are discussed. 2 Do social evaluatio ns (i.e., the attributes of the valencedominan ce model) impact deepfake detection ? H0: No H1: Social evaluations mediate the detection of deepfake faces. Specifically: a. Attractiveness, but not trustworthiness, predicts higher accuracy in judging faces as deepfake or real. b. Exploratory investigation of the mediating role of the remaining 11 attributes in deepfake detection. 300 participants will take part in the study allowing for > 98% statistical power when testing one of the thirteen predictors. If participants do fulfill the exclusion criteria, they will be substituted (see section Exclusion criteria).

The percentage of stimuli judged as deepfake will be computed, as well as participant-level accuracy and signal detection measure d′ as an index of discrimination sensibility. This procedure replicates the statistical methodology of Miller et al. (2023).

A stimulus-level lens model will be applied in order to investigate the attributes as simultaneous mediators of detection performances.

Power analysis with a medium effect size (Cohen's f = .15), based on studies using single attributes of the tested model (Miller et al., 2023; Tucciarelli et al., 2022), showed a power of 0.99, when testing 1 of a total of 13 predictors. The role of each of the thirteen attributes will be tested for significance adopting a statistical NHST approach (p < .05). Significant positive predictors = social evaluations impact correct deepfake detection. Significant negative predictors = that these attributes lead to faces being misjudged (see Miller et al., 2023).

H0: Deepfake detection is not based on social evaluations, disconfirming results on attractiveness by Miller et al. (2023) and Tucciarelli et al. (2022). H1: Significant predictors show a relevant role of social evaluations on deepfake detection: positive predictors improve detection of deepfake faces, negative predictors impair detection of deepfake faces.

H0: These results suggest that social evaluations may not be relevant for deepfake detection performances, suggesting that deepfake detection might not rely on social components of decision-making processes.

H1: Results provide the first theory-driven evidence of the role of social evaluations in deepfake detection, stressing the role of social components in decision-making. H2.a. Neither attractiveness nor trustworthiness predicted accuracy in the deepfake detection task. H2.b. Three other attributes were shown to directly and negatively predict accuracy, namely, weirdness, caringness and intelligence. Moreover, indirect effects of Stimulus Type through attribute ratings revealed that, whilst caringness and intelligence were negatively associated with accuracy of deepfake stimuli, weirdness, on the other hand, revealed to be positively associated with the detection of deepfake faces. Thus, specific social components seem to play a role in decision making.

Introduction

How do humans form social evaluations of deepfake faces?

Humans make social inferences about people they interact with, based on facial appearances (e.g., Richtie et al., 2017). These impressions can influence relevant social outcomes such as juridical sentences or economic decisions (e.g., Ahola et al., 2009; Li et al., 2023). Willis and Todorov (2006) reveal the rapidity of facial trait judgments, emphasising the formation of immediate impressions based on implicit dimensions, like trustworthiness and aggressiveness. In examining the basis of face evaluation in humans, Oosterhof and Todorov (2008) elaborated a model whose main dimensions, valence and dominance, represent the main elements for judging neutral faces. They describe valence as the observer's perception of the face's trustworthiness, which predicts the decision of approach or avoidance; dominance, on the other hand, represents the perception based on characteristics of weakness or physical strength. Oosterhof and Todorov (2008) derived their valence-dominance model from a principal components analysis (PCA) of ratings of 66 faces for 13 different traits (aggressiveness, attractiveness, caringness, confidence, dominance, emotional stability, intelligence, meanness, responsibility, sociability, trustworthiness, unhappiness, and weirdness). The first component explained 63% of the variance in trait ratings, strongly correlated with rated trustworthiness, and weakly correlated with rated dominance. The second component explained 18% of the variance in trait ratings, strongly correlated with rated dominance, and not correlated with rated trustworthiness.

The model has been validated across eleven world regions, revealing important regional differences in the cognitive process of face perceptions (Jones et al., 2021). Tzschaschel et al. (2022) have also examined the evaluation of whole-body photographs, replicating Oosterhof and Todorov's (2008) study and strengthening the valence-dominance model as a powerful theoretical model to explain social perceptions of bodies. The traits investigated by Willis and Todorov (2006) in regard to unfamiliar faces were presented for different timings (100, 500, 1000 milliseconds), allowing for the conclusion that the formation of the participants' first impression requires 100 milliseconds. In fact, research has widely replicated that our first impression does not change beyond 200 milliseconds (Ballew & Todorov 2007; Bar et al., 2006; Borkenau et al., 2009; Porter et al., 2008; Todorov et al., 2009; Todorov et al., 2015). Moreover, literature has shown that physical characteristics of faces (e.g., face shape) can influence first impressions, leading to overgeneralization when judging people's appearances (Zebrowitz, 2017; however, see Jones & Jaeger, 2019 and Lee et al., 2021 for recent contrasting evidence).

Recent evidence reported that people not only form first impressions from facial appearances of humans but also from synthetic faces (e.g., Nightingale & Farid, 2022). Research has shown computer-generated faces to be evaluated as less attractive (Patel & MacDorman, 2015) or less trustworthy (Balas & Pacella, 2017) compared to real faces, whilst other studies did not find significant differences in immediate processing (i.e., no difference in trustworthiness: Patel & MacDorman, 2015; no difference in attractiveness: Cheetham et al., 2015).

Interestingly, the valence-dominance model has also been applied on synthetic faces (created with the FaceGen application) by Balas et al. (2018). The authors found the model to be sufficiently applicable on FaceGen faces, which are synthetic faces created on the basis of the corresponding human faces. However, FaceGen and other synthetic faces are created on the basis of feature points of real faces (i.e., distances between six to eight face parts), and the model is learned from a set of textured 3D scans of heads (Blanz & Vetter, 2003). These characteristics allow for mistakes in the produced images (Crookes et al., 2015), which can be perceived by humans and, in turn, may influence the first impressions. Crookes et al. (2015), for instance, highlight that "the most notable difference between these CG faces (computer-generated faces, i.e., synthetic faces) and face photographs is that the CG faces appear to lack fine-grained surface texture information and imperfections that are usually present in photographic face stimuli. This gives the impression of these faces being somewhat artificial and unreal" (p. 2). Differently from these synthetic faces, Artificial Intelligence (AI) has more recently allowed the creation of deepfake faces, which are generated by constantly new deep learning algorithms, able to create increasingly more realistic faces (e.g., Papa et al., 2023). The realism of the deepfake faces and the possibility to interact with AI generated content lead to new questions about how people evaluate AI products and, in turn, could interact with them (Gil et al., 2023). Nightingale and Farid (2022) asked their participants to rate the trustworthiness of real and deepfake faces, and found deepfake faces to be judged as significantly more trustworthy compared to real faces. Moreover, Miller et al. (2023) found deepfake faces to be judged as more attractive compared to real faces.

A complete account of how people form first impressions about deepfake faces would be of paramount importance from both a theoretical and applied point of view, for both computer-and cognitive sciences. Thus, with the present study we aim at providing a theoretical framework of how people form first impressions about deepfake faces, by validating the valence-dominance model on deepfake faces.

Do social evaluations impact deepfake detection?

Recent evidence has highlighted new ethical and societal challenges associated with humans' inability to distinguish deepfake and real faces (i.e., threats to one's digital identity; e.g., De Ruiter, 2021; Shen et al., 2021). Engineering and informatic sciences have shown that human ability to discriminate between real and deepfake faces ranges from chance level (e.g., Nightingale & Farid, 2022; Shen et al., 2021) to up to 60% -75% accuracy (e.g., Bray et al., 2023; Maiano et al., 2024; Tarchi et al., 2023). This apparent human difficulty in the distinction of real and deepfake photos has raised the question on which variables contribute to judging faces as real, even if they are deepfake. In this line, psychological research has recently focused on the impact of first impressions (see above) on deepfake detection. Miller et al. (2023) found higher rated attractiveness to be associated with the categorization of faces as deepfake, i.e. leading to higher detection accuracy of deepfake faces but, at the same time, higher miscategorization of human faces as AI-generated content. Similarly, Tucciarelli et al. (2022) have investigated whether first impressions can contribute to misjudging deepfake (i.e., Generative Adversarial Network; GAN) faces as real. More specifically, they asked three groups of participants to rate their first impressions of 100 photos (50% real, 50% GAN) in regard to attractiveness, expressiveness and trustworthiness. Subsequently, a detection task was performed by different participants on the same stimulus set (50% real and 50% deepfake). Results showed, in line with Miller et al. (2023), that more attractive faces were less likely categorised as real. Interestingly, no significant impact of expressiveness or trustworthiness was found on categorization accuracy in the detection task.

Further evidence for the impact of first impressions on detection accuracy stems from Maiano et al. (2024). The authors measured likeability when first perceiving real vs. deepfake faces, and found higher likeability of photos to be associated with misjudgements of deepfake faces as real. In line with this, also Ng (2023) found that first impressions can be related to the categorization of deepfake faces as real. More specifically, the author showed higher perceived trustworthiness to be associated with higher perceived realness of the video stimuli.

In line with these preliminary and contrasting results on the role of first impressions in the evaluation of (deepfake) faces, the second aim of the present study is to investigate which attributes lead faces to be judged as deepfake (even if they are real). To our knowledge, this is the first study aimed to systematically answer this research question based on a well-established theoretical framework of social perception, i.e. the valence-dominance model. More specifically, we aim at investigating how the thirteen attributes of this model contribute to the understanding of how (deepfake) faces are detected.

The scarcity of literature in this regard, leads to the aim of replicating the most recent evidence on the impact of attractiveness and trustworthiness (e.g., Miller et al., 2023; Tucciarelli et al., 2022) on face detection, and extending this evidence to the remaining valence-dominance attributes. By taking into account both detection processes and face evaluations, our study will provide insights into whether certain attributes serve as cognitive basis that can impair or enhance deepfake detection. This allows to clarify the underlying mechanisms of deepfake detection and may contribute to designing interventions improving detection skills. Ethical and societal implications will be discussed.

Hypotheses

The study aims to (1) validate the valence-dominance model on deepfake faces and (2) to investigate how the valence-dominance traits impact human performance in deepfake face detection.

Thus, our hypotheses can be summarised in two different sets, as follows: 1.

The component structure of the valence-dominance model for human faces extends to deepfake faces. a. The component structure of the valence-dominance model for human faces also extends to faces categorized as deepfake.

2. Social evaluations impact deepfake face detection. Specifically: a. Attractiveness, but not trustworthiness, predicts higher accuracy in judging faces as deepfake or real. b. Aggressiveness, caringness, confidence, dominance, emotional stability, intelligence, meanness, responsibility, sociability, unhappiness, and weirdness may impact detection accuracy of deepfake and real faces. To our knowledge, no existing literature has investigated these variables in the context of deepfake or synthetic face detection, thus, directions and strengths of these relationships are part of the exploratory aims of this study.

Methods

Ethics.

The research has received approval from the Departmental ethics committee of Sapienza University of Rome [UOR: SI000092 -Classif. VII/15]. All participants provided informed consent.

All data is stored at https://osf.io/tj7cr/files/5dt3v.

Materials and Procedure.

We aimed at replicating the Oosterhof and Todorov's method and primary analysis also on deepfake faces. Stimuli in our study came from an open-access, full-colour, standardised image set of real faces (3DSK face set, De Bruine & Jones, 2020), and from a deepfake face image set. The image set of deepfake faces was produced ad hoc through the application of a specific algorithm and is accessible for further investigations. More specifically, the set of deepfake face images was produced through a specific artificial intelligence algorithm based on the diffusion model technology (Rombach et al., 2022), which was made accessible for further investigation (https://github.com/LucaCorvitto/VDM-on-deepfake-faces). In more detail, similarly to Papa et al. (2023), realistic deepfake faces were generated through a timely engineering strategy that allows generating artificial faces based on a textual description, i.e. Diffusion Models (DM). This applied methodology has several advantages: whilst alternatives like Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs; Goodfellow et al., 2014) have been known for their exceptional ability to generate high-quality images and were used extensively in generating deepfakes manipulating people's faces, they have been demonstrated to fail in covering the entire training data distribution. DMs, instead, are able to produce even better realistic images than GANs (Guarnera et al., 2024) and offer advantages in terms of better control over the generative process and the ability to generate images with a wide range of styles and content.

In particular, in the present study, we build upon the framework of Papa et al. (2023) while adopting a modified prompt-engineering strategy to align generated images with the real-face dataset. Exploiting the controllability of diffusion models, allowing flexible and fine-grained manipulation compared to earlier generative approaches, we define the following constraints: (1) passport-style portraits with strictly frontal view; (2) uniform white background, consistent with the real data acquisition setting, and (3) explicit control of facial attributes via structured prompts and negative prompting to reduce artifacts and biases. These adaptations enable closer adherence to the visual characteristics of real samples while maintaining high image quality. The decision to adopt a new set of deepfake stimuli stems from the necessity of highly standardised face images, comparable to the available standardised real face images, in contrast with previous studies on deepfake detection (Nightingale & Farid, 2022; Tucciarelli et al., 2022). As in Oosterhof and Todorov study, the individuals depicted in the real and deepfake images pose looking directly in front of them with a neutral expression, and all of the background and lighting are constant across images. After a first selection from the complete deepfake image set, in order to standardize deepfake face stimuli making them comparable to real face stimuli, the images were edited in the following way: 1) removal of (grey) background, 2) if applicable, removal of torso, 3) if applicable, removal of visible pony-tails or braids (in case of tied-up hair of females).

Finally, the image sets entirely consisted of Caucasian people. The deepfake and the real sets of faces are respectively constituted by 30 (50%) male faces with short hair, no beard, and no accessories, and 30 (50%) female faces with short or tied-up hair, and no accessories. Thus, the complete image set consisted of 120 faces (50% real, 50% male) with a resolution of 512 x 728 pixels (see osf.io/tj7cr/files/osfstorage for our final deepfake stimuli).

In our study, Italian adult raters were randomly assigned to rate only one of the thirteen attributes tested by Oosterhof and Todorov, on the full stimuli set (120 faces). Thus, each face has ratings for each of the thirteen attributes. Participants firstly completed a short questionnaire requesting demographic information (sex, age, ethnicity), and information about the device used to complete the task will be recorded. The task was carried out online on PsychoPy via Pavlovia (Peirce et al., 2019). Participants carried the task out on their personal computers with the instruction to sit approximately 40 cm distant from the screen. The face stimuli had the same stimulus dimensions for each participant, and all images were presented on the top center of the screen with a stimulus size of 13.5 x 10.5 cm.

Each trial consisted of the randomised presentation of one of the 120 faces that participants were asked to judge as fake or real as quickly and accurately as possible. Participants were asked to select one of the two response options (deepfake vs. real) that were presented horizontally on the bottom of the screen, counterbalancing the left/right order of the two responses across participants. Additionally, each participant was asked to rate one of the 13 attributes using scales ranging from 1 (Not at all) to 9 (Very) for all 120 faces, at their own pace. In line with the cross-cultural study by Jones et al. (2021), dictionary definitions of the trait the participant was assigned to, were provided in order to reduce potential cultural (i.e., Italian) and between-participants biases in interpreting the attribute labels. Within each trial, the order of detection task (deepfake vs. real) and attribute rating were counterbalanced across participants, with half of the participants of each group carrying out first the detection task and subsequently the attribute rating.

Example trial including the detection task and attribute rating

Four additional faces (50% real, 50% male) were administered for attentional checks, for which participants were asked to state the presence or absence of specific face characteristics (i.e., beard, glasses). Data on these four faces was only used as exclusion criteria (See Exclusions section), and was not part of the set of analysed data. Each participant completed the block of rating trials (120 faces and 4 attentional checks) twice, allowing us to report test-retest reliabilities of ratings. For analyses on the valence-dominance attributes, ratings from the first and the second blocks were averaged whilst, to investigate detection performances, the main analyses only took into account the first block of accuracy ratings. Additionally, response times were recorded, as per default PsychoPy settings, for each answer (both detection and attribute ratings). However, as analysis on response times exceeded the aim of the current study, our publicly available data will allow other researchers and our research group to use them in secondary analyses of the published data.

Power analysis. We ran two different power analyses for the two different aims of the research project.

In order to assess the power that we expect to replicate the valence-dominance model (Oosterhof & Todorov, 2008) on deepfake faces (aim 1), we repeated the same simulation power analysis as in Jones et al. (2021), run on 60 randomly selected real face stimuli (i.e., planned size of the deepfake and real stimulus sets, respectively). This choice was made based on the unavailability of public data on deepfake faces, as the valence-dominance model has not been applied on deepfake faces yet. Results showed that 85.6% of these analyses matched the criteria for replicating Oosterhof and Todorov's findings. This demonstrates that the number of our stimuli (60 faces) will give us more than 85% power to replicate the two-component model of Oosterhof and Todorov (2008); thus, if the model applies also to deepfake faces (which we expect to), we would detect the effect with a power of 85.6%. Our adapted code taken from Jones et al. (2021) is available at https://osf.io/tj7cr/?view_only=7fc853b03c9d4b03a3b111d6412a0e3a (RRStage1/RR1_poweranalysis.R).

For our exploratory aim of assessing the component structure of faces categorized as deepfakes, we estimated statistical power using a Monte Carlo simulation on our collected data, shifting from the preregistered approach. This shift was required because the original method (i.e., based on the mean number of faces judged as deepfakes) overlooked a critical reduction in sample size at the rater level.

Whilst the mean number of faces categorized as real (M = 61.67, SD = 15.22) and deepfake (M = 58.50, SD = 14.88) was adequate, all 120 stimuli were ultimately judged as both real and fake by participants.

Consequently, the actual number of raters per attribute and stimulus fell below the planned 23 participants. In accordance with our Stage 1 Registered Report, we established that the exploratory PCA would be reported and interpreted only if the simulated power reached the 80% threshold. The code is available at: (RRStage2/simulation_exploratory_RR2. R).

In regard to the second aim of the present study (investigating the impact of the 13 attributes on the accuracy of (mis)judging faces as real), we carried out a second power analysis. In line with Miller et al. (2023), we computed a power analysis for linear multiple regression fixed models using the number of faces (N = 120) as sample size. Using the function "pwrss.f.reg" in the R package pwrss (Bulus, 2023), expecting a medium effect size of Cohen's f = .15 (Miller et al., 2023; Tucciarelli et al., 2022) and setting alpha to .05, we found a power of 0.98869, when testing 1 of a total of 13 predictors. The code is available at https://osf.io/tj7cr/?view_only=7fc853b03c9d4b03a3b111d6412a0e3a (RRStage1/RR1_poweranalysis.R).

Participants

Simulations determined that we should obtain at least 23 different raters for each of the 13 traits (the code is available at: https://osf.io/tj7cr/?view_only=7fc853b03c9d4b03a3b111d6412a0e3a (RRStage1/RR1_samplesize_simulation.R). To our knowledge, only Tucciarelli et al. (2022) examined the detection of deepfake faces in relation to attributes of the valence-dominance model, also making their data publicly available. However, these authors measured only two traits of the model in relation to deepfake faces, namely attractiveness and trustworthiness. Adopting the same code developed by De Bruine and Jones (2018), the simulation analysis was run on the ratings of attractiveness and trustworthiness from Tucciarelli et al. (2022), respectively for 50 real and 50 deepfake faces. First, we sampled from a population of 30 raters, each of whom had rated the trustworthiness of 50 deepfake faces; these simulations showed that 94% of 1,000 random samples of 21 raters produced good or excellent interrater reliability coefficients (Cronbach's αs >.80; Table 1, Figure 1 in Supplementary Materials, RR Stage 1). We then repeated these simulations sampling from a population of 30 raters, each of whom rated the trustworthiness of 50 real faces, showing that 95% of 1,000 random samples of 23 raters produced good or excellent interrater reliability coefficients (Cronbach's αs >.80; Table 2, Figure 2 in Supplementary Materials,

RR Stage 1).

We repeated the same procedure for judgments of attractiveness on 50 deepfake and 50 real faces.

Simulations showed that more than 99% of 1,000 random samples of 20 raters produced good or excellent interrater reliability coefficients (Cronbach's αs >.80), respectively for attractiveness of deepfake faces (Table 3, Figure 3, in Supplementary Materials RR Stage 1), and for attractiveness of real faces (Table 4, Figure 4 in Supplementary Materials, RR Stage 1). Thus, by applying a conservative approach (i.e., simulation analysis was run on ratings referring to 50 faces, whilst our dataset comprised 60 stimuli for the real and deepfake faces, respectively), averages of ratings from 23 or more raters produce reliable scores. We therefore planned to test at least 300 raters in total.

The final sample included 311 Italian participants (Age: M = 37.04 years, SD = 12.58; 148 females) recruited via Prolific (compensation ≃ 7 € / hour). The inclusion criteria to take part were as follows:

Italian native speakers, aged from 18 to 65 years, normal to corrected vision, no psychiatric or neurological disorders.

Analysis plan

Data was analysed based on the two main aims of the study, all analyses were carried out on RStudio (R version 4.4.0, 2024-04-24). The final scripts applied on our data are publicly available on Open Science Framework (OSF): osf.io/tj7cr/files/ktmzy (RR Stage 2 -revised /RR2_revised.R)

1. Applying the valence-dominance model to the evaluation of deepfake faces.

Two distinct Principal Component Analyses (PCA) have been conducted on averaged attribute ratings for real and deepfake faces, using the psych package (Revelle & Revelle, 2024). First, we aimed at replicating the PCA conducted by Oosterhof and Todorov (2008) in order to assess the validity of their theoretical framework across both real and deepfake faces. Thus, we computed the average ratings for each of the thirteen traits for every face. Subsequently, the dataset was splitted in two different datasets for real and deepfake faces, respectively. For each dataset, PCA without rotation was applied to the mean ratings, consistent with the methodology employed by Oosterhof and Todorov (2008). As in this original study, we retained and interpreted the components with eigenvalues greater than 1.0 (see also e.g., Jockwitz et al., 2021; Turnbull et al., 2021).

1.1 Criteria for replicating Oosterhof and Todorov's valence-dominance model in deepfake faces.

Similarly to previous studies validating the valence-dominance model (e.g., Jones et al., 2021; Shiramizu et al., 2022), we adopted three different criteria (based on PCA values) to assess the replication of Oosterhof and Todorov's valence-dominance model within deepfake faces: 1) presence of eigenvalues greater than 1.0 for the first two components, 2) the first component correlates strongly with trustworthiness (λ > .7) and weakly with dominance (λ < .5), and 3), whilst the second component correlates strongly with dominance (λ > .7) and weakly with trustworthiness (λ < .5). If these criteria are met for data on deepfake faces, we conclude that the primary pattern of the model is replicated. The same analysis was also conducted on ratings for real faces, in order to check for convergent validity.

Analysis was carried out following the code of Jones et al. (2021). See about:blank (RRStage1/RR1_plannedmainanalysis.R) for the planned adapted code and osf.io/tj7cr/files/ktmzy(RR Stage 2 -revised /RR2_revised.R) for the final applied code.

1.2. Does the categorization of faces as real or deepfake impact the valence-dominance ratings differently?

To control for a possible impact of the categorization of faces as either real or deepfake (i.e., detection judgements) on the attribute ratings of the valence-dominance model, exploratory analysis was carried out. In case of sufficient power (see Power analysis ), additional PCAs based on the categorization of the participants were computed following the same criteria as in 1.1 and are subsequently compared to the PCAs on actual deepfake and real faces (see osf.io/tj7cr/files/k9guf (RRStage1/R1/RR1_plannedmainanalysisR1.

R) for the planned code and osf.io/tj7cr/files/ktmzy(RRStage2 -revised / RR2_revised.R) for the final applied code.

2. Testing if Oosterhof and Todorov's valence-dominance model is related to human performances

in detecting real and deepfake faces.

In line with the statistical methodology of Miller et al. (2023), we calculated the participant-level Signal Detection Measure, D-prime (d′), as an index of discrimination sensibility between deepfake and real faces (using the psycho package; Makowski, 2018), as well as mean accuracy levels divided by stimulus type. Complementary stimulus-level analyses are reported, as well as stimulus-level mean ratings for each of the thirteen attributes separately, in order to illustrate descriptive statistics. Moreover, we calculated the percentage of participants who judge each face as deepfake. Higher percentage values indicate that more participants have judged a face as deepfake. Stimulus type (i.e., deepfake or real faces) is dummy-coded (0 = real faces,1 = deepfake faces).

In order to gain an overall understanding on the potential relationship between the valence-dominance model and human detection performances, we first ran a simple regression model in which the PCA scores (i.e., of the obtained components in 1.1) predict the above described detection-related variable (i.e., accuracy).

Then, to determine which attributes make faces look deepfake (despite their actual stimulus type), we constructed a multiple linear regression model predicting the detection accuracy of participants from the thirteen stimulus-level attribute ratings.

In line with Miller et al. (2023), we then aimed at applying a Brunswikian lens model on the regression model (Brunswik, 1956; Hall et al., 2019) to reveal how each of the thirteen attributes contributed to faces being (mis)judged as deepfake. Constructing a stimulus-level lens model (using lavaan; Rosseel, 2012) allowed us to investigate the attributes as simultaneous mediators. This explains the correspondence between the deepfake or real nature of faces and participants' ability to identify their category, thereby distinguishing between trait validity (differences in the psychological attributes of real or deepfake face evaluation) and trait utilisation (the extent to which each trait contributes to faces being correctly categorized). In this model, face type was the focal predictor (real = 0 vs. deepfake = 1), the mean ratings (across blocks) of the thirteen attributes were included as simultaneous mediators, and stimulus-level mean accuracy, derived from first-block detection responses, represented the outcome variable.

All attributes were allowed to freely correlate with each other, which led to a fully saturated model that perfectly fits our data. Multicollinearity was tested for with the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF, e.g., Chan et al., 2022) with a VIF > 5 indicating problematic multicollinearity, e.g., Choi et al., 2023; Montgomery et al., 2021). See osf.io/tj7cr/files/k9guf (RRStage1/RR1_plannedmainanalysisR1. R) for the planned analysis including the adapted lens model code by Miller et al. (2023) and osf.io/tj7cr/files/ktmzy (RR Stage 2 -revised / RR2_revised.R) for the final code.

3. Unregistered exploratory analyses

Regarding the simple regression model in which the PCA scores predict accuracy, we additionally included Stimulus Type as a predictor in interaction with both Valence and Dominance principal components to test for potential differential effects of Stimulus Type.

Furthermore, to evaluate the robustness of preregistered findings, sensitivity analyses are reported.

Specifically, the multiple regression and Brunswikian lens model were also estimated adopting data exclusively from the first block of ratings. This controlled for potential confounds related to the second rating judgment, which did not necessarily correspond to the same detection response as in the first block. Finally, we refitted the regression and lens model removing attributes with low internal consistency (see Data Quality checks). interrater agreement (i.e., Cronbach's α, test-retest reliability) for each attribute in both real and 353 deepfake faces. If the α coefficient was greater than .70, attributes were included in the analysis. 354

Importantly, three attributes related to deepfake stimuli reached α lower than .70 (i.e., trustworthiness, 355 emotional stability and intelligence) and were excluded from PCA but not from other analyses; see 356 Finally, in order to control for potential confounding effects of task order (detection task and rating task), an exploratory MANOVA was carried out including the ratings of the valence-dominance attributes predicted by the task order (detection-rating or rating-detection). A significant main effect of order was encountered (F(13, 226) = 87.46, p < .001). More precisely, single univariate models showed significant order effects on the following attributes: dominance (p < .0001), emotional stability (p = .001), intelligence (p = .001), caringness (p < .001), confidence (p = .045) and sociability (p < .001) whilst the remaining attributes were not impacted by order (all ps > .279).

Exclusions.

Participants who failed to correctly respond to two or more attention check trials were rejected and automatically replaced during the data collection phase (N = 133). Additionally, during data collection 287 participants returned their submission or timed out. Following this phase, data from participants who did not complete all 120 ratings in the first block of trials (N = 3) or who provided the same ratings for ≥ 75% of the stimuli (N = 13) were excluded from data analysis (see Jones et al., 2021). Finally, test-retest reliability was calculated at participant level, and participants reporting values equal to 0 or negative (N = 7) were excluded from the dataset (see Oh et al., 2019; Todorov & Oh, 2021). Overall, participants excluded after the first recruiting section were replaced through a second session, reaching the required sample size of minimum 300 participants (see Participants section).

Results

Confirmatory results

Applying the valence-dominance model to the evaluation of deepfake faces.

First, mean trait ratings for the 10 included attributes (see Data quality section for the excluded 386 attributes) related to deepfake faces were subject to PCA without rotation. This analysis revealed two 387 Principal Components (PCs). Eigenvalues were equal to 5.26 and 2.23, respectively and explained 53% 388 and 22% of the variance in ratings, respectively. Factor loadings of the individual traits on all PCs are 389 shown in Table 3. 390 391 Table 3.392 Components loadings for both real and deepfake faces 393 394 Real Deepfake Trait PC1 PC2 PC3 PC1 PC2 Aggressiveness -.74 .59 .14 .92 .02 Attractiveness .61 .58 -.32 .56 .76 Caringness .91 -.20 .24 -.85 .38 Confidence .30 .74 .50 .78 .53 Dominance -.06 .93 .23 .86 .39 Emotional stability .88 .08 -.14 --Intelligence .76 .46 -.28 --Meanness -.83 .41 .17 .93 .00 Responsibility .91 .09 -.13 -.56 .46 Sociability .74 -.26 .52 -.78 .46 Trustworthiness .90 -.14 -.06 --Unhappiness -.72 .05 -.63 .48 -.61 Weirdness -.64 -.47 .39 -.08 -.53 SS loadings 6.98 2.83 1.44 5.26 2.23 Proportion Var .54 .22 .11 .53 .22 Cumulative Var .54 .75 .87 .53 .75 Proportion Explained .62 .25 .13 .70 .30 Cumulative Proportion .62 .87 1.00 .70 1.00

Inconsistent with previous research using real faces as stimuli, the first PC was highly correlated with traits such as aggressiveness (λ = .92) and meanness (λ = .93), and the second PC was the highest correlated with attractiveness (λ = .76) but weakly correlated with meanness and aggressiveness. Thus, following our preregistered criteria, our reduced 10-attribute PCA yielded two components with a loading structure that did not resemble the registered valence-dominance pattern. For subsequent analyses however, in line with previous research showing the opposite pattern of results (e.g., Jones et al., 2021; Shiramizu et al., 2022), we labelled the encountered PCs Dominance (PC1) and Valence (PC2), respectively. Please note that this decision represents a post hoc interpretation of the loading patterns.

Applying the valence-dominance model to the evaluation of real faces

Mean trait ratings of the thirteen valence-dominance attributes related to real faces were subject to PCA without rotation. This analysis revealed three PCs, with the first two components having eigenvalues equal to 6.98 and 2.82 and explaining 54% and 22% of the variance, respectively. The third component had an eigenvalue of 1.44 and explained 11% of the variance in ratings, with sociability and unhappiness loading on this component (but also cross-loading on the first component). This result is similar to the findings by Jones et al. (2021) who hesitated to interpret this component due to cross-loading of the traits (on PC1) and the explanation of a small proportion of additional variance. Finally, as shown in Table 3, the first PC was strongly marked by trustworthiness (λ = .90), responsibility (λ = .91) and caringness (λ = .91), whilst the second PC was strongly correlated with dominance (λ = .93).

Furthermore, PC1 correlated weakly with dominance (λ = -.06) and PC2 correlated weakly with trustworthiness (λ = -.14). Overall, the planned criteria for replicating the valence-dominance model were fulfilled in our participants' sample and we named PC1 Valence and PC2 Dominance, in line with literature.

Testing if Oosterhof and Todorov's valence-dominance model is related to human performances in detecting real and deepfake faces.

Overall, participants showed a mean d' of 1.25 ± 1.52. Accuracy for deepfake faces was .67 ± .13 and for real faces was .70 ± .10. Complementary stimulus-level analyses are reported (accuracy and mean ratings) for each of the thirteen attributes separately in the Supplementary Materials (2, Table 2.1; The regression model in which the PCA scores related to Valence and Dominance predict accuracy, showed significant main effects of Dominance loadings (F(1) = 24.45, p <.001, η² = .17), revealing that higher Dominance loadings predicted significantly higher accuracy. No significant effect was found for Valence loadings (p = .154).

Attractiveness and Trustworthiness

Then, the multiple linear regression model predicting the detection accuracy of participants from the thirteen stimulus-level mean attribute ratings (i.e., across the two blocks), was statistically significant, accounting for 36.83% of the variance in detection accuracy (F(13, 106) = 4.75, p < .001, R² adjusted = .29), with both attractiveness (β = -.122, SE = .28, t = -.43, p = .666) and trustworthiness (β = .266, SE = .18, t = 1.44, p = .152) ratings not significantly modulating detection accuracy. See Exploratory results for full description of all attributes (Other attributes).

Finally, the Brunswikian lens model accounted for 42% of variance in our data (R² = .420), showing that the deepfake nature of stimuli was associated with higher ratings of both attractiveness (b = 1.74, SE = 0.09, z = 19.60, p < .001) and trustworthiness (b = 1.08, SE = 0.15, z = 7.11, p < .001). Regarding attribute utilization, the model indicated that participants did not rely neither on trustworthiness (p = .706) nor on attractiveness (p = .852). No significant indirect effects emerged through the subjective rating of attractiveness (p = .852) and trustworthiness (p = .707). See Exploratory results for the full description of all attributes (Other attributes).

Exploratory results

Does the categorization of faces as real or deepfake impact the valence-dominance ratings differently?

Faces categorized as deepfake Results of Monte Carlo power analysis simulated on our dataset showed a power of 99.20%. Cronbach's alpha on attribute ratings could not be reliably computed for three specific attributes (i.e., weirdness, intelligence, and emotional stability); consequently, these attributes were excluded from the subsequent PCA (see Supplementary Materials 1.2, RR Stage2). The PCA run on faces categorized as deepfake revealed two distinct components with eigenvalues greater than 1. Specifically, the first component had an eigenvalue of 6.45, explaining 64% of the total variance, whereas the second component showed an eigenvalue of 1.44, accounting for an additional 14% of the variance. In terms of factor loadings, PC1 loaded strongly on trustworthiness (λ = .82) and weakly on dominance (λ = .30). Conversely, PC2 displayed a robust loading on dominance (λ = .88) and a weak relationship with trustworthiness (λ = -.05). See Table 4. These findings are consistent with the registered valence-dominance pattern for faces perceived as deepfake.

.82 1.00 Faces categorized as real Monte Carlo simulation power analysis was carried out on our dataset aiming at verifying the necessary power to replicate the valence-dominance model in faces judged as real (independently of their actual nature). The power analysis showed that among 1000 simulations only 208 samples were able to strictly replicate the valence dominance model in faces judged as real, thus yielding a power of 20.80 %, thus in line with the preregistered protocol, PCA is not reported and interpreted here. Testing if Oosterhof and Todorov's valence-dominance model is related to human performances in detecting real and deepfake faces.

Other attributes

The multiple linear regression model predicting the detection accuracy of participants from the thirteen stimulus-level mean attribute ratings (i.e., across the two blocks) also showed that higher intelligence ratings were associated with lower detection accuracy (β = -.704, SE = .20, t = -3.58, p < .001), see Figure 2. Furthermore, although higher dominance ratings were positively associated with detection accuracy, this effect did not reach statistical significance (β = .38, SE = .20, t = 1.91, p = .058). Other effects were not significant (ps > .118).

Standardized coefficients of the attribute ratings predicting detection performance (i.e., accuracy)

Finally, the Brunswikian lens model showed that the real or deepfake nature of facial stimuli significantly predicted all mediators (ps < .001), except for dominance (p = .665). As illustrated in Figure 3, the deepfake nature of stimuli was associated with higher ratings of caringness, confidence, emotional stability, intelligence, responsibility, and sociability. On the other hand, lower ratings for deepfake stimuli were found regarding weirdness, aggressiveness, unhappiness, and meanness (see Supplementary Materials 3, RR Stage 2, for the complete statistical descriptions). Regarding attribute utilization, the model indicated that participants relied significantly on weirdness, caringness, and intelligence. Specifically, overall detection accuracy significantly decreased with increasing ratings of weirdness (β = -.77, SE = .30, z = -2.60, p = .009), caringness (β = -.45, SE = .21, z = -2.15, p = .032) and intelligence (β = -.92, SE = .19, z = -4.89, p < .001). No other facial attributes exerted a significant direct impact on accuracy (ps > .179). Additionally, a significant negative direct effect of stimulus type on accuracy was observed (β = -.83, SE = .51, z = -3.27, p = .001), indicating that deepfake (vs. real) faces were associated with impaired detection performance independently of the attributes.

Finally, significant negative indirect effects emerged through the subjective rating of caringness (β = -0.28, SE = .26, z = -2.08, p = .038) and intelligence (β = -.67, SE = .30, z = -4.52, p < .001), showing them to be associated with impaired detection of deepfake stimuli. Conversely, a positive indirect effect emerged through weirdness (β = .70, SE = .54, z = 2.59, p = .010), with deepfake stimuli being detected more accurately. The total effect of the model was not significant (β = -.12, SE = .18, z = -1.36, p = .172). Brunswikian lens model testing contributions of each attribute to detection accuracy, with type of stimulus (left) being the focal predictor (real = 0 vs. deepfake = 1), the thirteen attributes (middle) the simultaneous mediators, and detection accuracy the dependent variable. Finally, multicollinearity analysis applying the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) revealed indexes ranging from 6.47 (trustworthiness) to 24.24 (emotional stability), indicating partially problematic multicollinearity (see Supplementary Materials 3.1, RR Stage 2, for complete VIF statistics).

Exploratory unregistered analyses

The regression model in which the PCA scores related to Valence and Dominance predict accuracy in interaction with Stimulus Type, showed significant main effects of Dominance loadings (F(1) = 82.45, p <.001, η² = .23), revealing that higher Dominance loadings predicted significantly higher accuracy (see Figure 4A). Stimulus type was not significant (p =.081; Real faces: M = .70 ± .10; Deepfake faces: M = .67 ± .13). No significant effect was found for Valence loadings (p = .165). Furthermore, a significant interaction effect was encountered between Dominance and Stimulus type (F(1) = 48.42, p <.001, η² = .30), but not between Valence and Stimulus type (p = .787). Post hoc analysis on the interaction effect between Dominance and Stimulus type, with Bonferroni correction, showed that, whilst for Deepfake faces higher Dominance predicted higher accuracy levels (trend = .10, SE = .01, df = 114, t = 9.08, p < .001), this was not true for Real faces (p = .897), see Figure 4B.

Predicted accuracy levels by A) Dominance component ratings and B) the interaction between

Dominance component ratings and Stimulus Type (Real vs. Fake)

Sensitivity analysis testing the predicted detection accuracy from the thirteen stimulus-level attribute ratings stemming from the first block only, showed a similar pattern of results to the registered analyses.

Specifically, the regression model accounted for 30.72% of the variance in detection accuracy (F(13, 106) = 3.62, p < .001, R² adjusted = .22). Higher dominance ratings were significantly associated with higher accuracy (β = .39, SE = .17, t = 2.36, p = .020), whilst higher intelligence ratings were associated with lower detection accuracy (β = -.43, SE = .17, t = -2.58, p = .011). Other effects were not significant (ps > .124). Finally, the application of the lens model to ratings stemming exclusively from the first block yielded an identical pattern of results as encountered in the preregistered analyses.

Moreover, sensitivity analyses including only the ten attributes with an encountered reliability of >.70 (i.e., excluding intelligence, trustworthiness, and emotional stability), showed that the regression model predicting detection accuracy was statistically significant, accounting for 28.76% of the variance (F(10, 109)=4.40, p < .001, R² adjusted = .22). Higher caringness ratings were associated with lower detection accuracy (β = -.456, SE = .23, t = -2.01, p = .047). Other effects were not significant (ps > .056).

Furthermore, the same sensitivity analysis on the Brunswikian lens model revealed that the ten attributes accounted for 30.3% of the variance in detection accuracy (R² = .303). The real or deepfake nature of facial stimuli significantly predicted all mediator attributes (ps < .001), except for dominance (p = .665).

Specifically, the deepfake nature of stimuli was associated with higher ratings of attractiveness, caringness, confidence, responsibility, and sociability. On the other hand, lower ratings for deepfake stimuli were associated with aggressiveness, meanness, unhappiness, and weirdness (Supplementary Materials 4 for the complete statistical descriptions). Regarding attribute utilization, the model indicated that participants relied significantly on caringness, with detection accuracy decreasing at higher ratings of caringness (β = -.552, SE = .22, z = -2.49, p = .013). No other facial attributes significantly modulated accuracy (ps > .099). Additionally, the direct effect of stimulus type on accuracy was not statistically significant (p = .101). Finally, a significant negative indirect effect of caringness was found (β = -.339, SE = .28, z = -2.39, p = .017). Other indirect effects were not significant (ps > .107). The total effect of the model was not significant (p = .172).

Discussion

This is the first study aiming at validating the valence-dominance model on deepfake faces, and concurrently investigating how these social traits impact human performance in deepfake face detection.

Our findings reveal that whilst it was not possible to completely replicate the component structure of the valence-dominance model to deepfake faces, according to the pre-registered pattern, (H1), it does regarding faces categorized as deepfake, irrespectively of their actual nature (H1a). Furthermore, regarding detection performances, higher dominance component loadings predicted significantly higher accuracy. Specifically, the unregistered exploratory results suggest that higher dominance loadings are associated with higher accuracy only for deepfake faces, while this was not true for real faces. Finally, a linear regression revealed higher intelligence ratings of the faces were associated with lower detection accuracy, in accordance with results of the Brunswikian lens model, overall showing that certain attributes of the valence-dominance model (i.e., intelligence, caringness and weirdness) play a role for the real/deepfake face detection accuracy. However, it should be noted that intelligence reached low reliability levels and, as a consequence, was excluded from sensitivity analyses.

Human social evaluation of (categorized) deepfake faces

Regarding our first set of hypotheses, the PCA on real faces successfully replicated the classic valencedominance model (Oosterhof & Todorov, 2008), confirming the psychometric reliability of our data within a Western European sample (see also Jones et al., 2021). Interestingly, when analysing deepfake faces, inconclusive findings were obtained by the reduced 10-attribute PCA, yielding two components with a loading structure that did not resemble the registered valence-dominance pattern, not allowing for providing support for H1. Whilst this inconclusive finding apparently contrasts with previous literature, replicating the valence-dominance model on CG-faces (e.g., Balas et al., 2017; Oosterhof & Todorov, 2008), at least three main methodological and theoretical divergences may account for these discrepancies.

First, previous investigations that simultaneously examined all traits of the valence-dominance model utilized computer-generated faces (e.g., FaceGen stimuli; Balas et al., 2017; Oosterhof & Todorov, 2008). The fact that those studies successfully replicated the model may suggest that the underlying generative technology plays a critical role in how artificial faces are socially evaluated. Unlike older computer-generated faces that are algorithmically morph-mapped from real human anatomy (e.g., Crookes et al., 2015), faces used in the present study were created by Diffusion Models, which synthesize faces from textual prompts. Consequently, despite their hyper-realism (Tucciarelli et al., 2022), they may lack the subtle, highly coordinated configuration of physical cues that humans implicitly leverage when evaluating faces, leading to different patterns of social evaluation. Indeed, within our paradigm, this may have particularly impacted traits such as trustworthiness, emotional stability, and intelligence, which were found to be characterized by low reliability, showing inconsistency of the social constructs in response to deepfake faces. Whilst the unreliability of these valence-related traits, and their consequential exclusion from the PCA, mathematically shifted the primary variance towards the dominance component, the unreliability of these traits warrants some further discussion. One possible explanation could be that attributes related to valence have an affective dimension with a stronger relational potential (e.g., avoiding or approaching; e.g., Oosterhof & Todorov, 2008). If in deepfake faces humans covertly perceive a mismatch between the stimulus and the potential to interact (e.g., less alive in the eyes; e.g., Miller et al., 2023), those social constructs may not apply in the same way they apply to real human faces. Lastly, one must also consider that our participants were actively engaged in a detection task, which potentially impacted their subsequent evaluations (e.g., Street, 2014). As is common in deception detection paradigms (Levine, 2014; Convertino et al., 2024), this explicit awareness of potential deception likely introduced a cognitive frame of suspicion, probably disrupting the spontaneous, automated social evaluation of face stimuli.

In agreement with this argument, Stockner et al. (2026) found attractiveness ratings to be affected by previous categorization responses of deepfake or real faces. Future research will be needed to specifically disentangle the underlying mechanisms responsible for the differential organization of valence-dominance attributes, and to verify whether specific attributes can indeed not be applied to deepfake faces.

Even more interestingly, and in contrast with the evaluations of objective deepfakes, the valencedominance model was fully replicated when data were analysed on faces subjectively categorized as deepfake, thereby supporting H1a. Overall, the encountered divergence between objective and subjective evaluations provides an interesting theoretical insight, suggesting a dissonance between bottom-up visual processing and top-down cognitive appraisal. When evaluating deepfake stimuli, bottom-up processing is based on the intrinsic characteristics of AI faces (e.g., inconsistent facial cues), breaking down the traditional dimensional structure of human social evaluation. Conversely, when participants identify a face as a deepfake, they likely engage a top-down, stereotypic social schema (e.g., Sütterlin et al., 2023). This schema may compensate for the immediate perceptual processes that would otherwise drive social-cognitive evaluations, ultimately aligning their ratings with the structured evaluation mechanics typical of real faces (e.g., "this face is artificial and deceptive, but if it was real, I would rate its weirdness as X"). The engagement of these top-down control processes would allow participants to organize social traits in a meaningful, highly structured manner, thereby avoiding cognitive overload (e.g., Yaya et al., 2024) and mitigating the covert cognitive dissonance between anomalous facial characteristics and subjective trait judgments. Whilst it was not the primary aim of the present study to disentangle the precise underlying mechanisms of this effect, future research should investigate how Response Times, as a potential index of underlying cognitive processes (Sternberg, 2004), within our dataset are associated with the evaluation and detection of actual versus perceived deepfake faces.

Impact of social evaluations on deepfake detection

Overall, in line with recent literature and meta-analytic findings (e.g., Maiano et al., 2024; Stockner et al., 2026), real faces were detected with significantly higher accuracy than deepfakes. More interestingly, the dominance component predicted detection accuracy, and the exploratory results revealed that this was true particularly for deepfake faces. This suggests that the apparently more relevant role of dominance-related attributes related to deepfake faces affects detection performances.

This can be interpreted to a certain extent in line with evolutionary theories showing that negative social attributes (such as danger) are linked to an increase in type I cognitive errors (i.e., more likely judging stimuli as deepfake), as the cost of committing a type II error (i.e., missing a potential negative stimulus) is much higher and can have important consequences (e.g., Haselton & Nette, 2006). However, it is worth noting that these results should be interpreted with caution considering that PCAs of real and deepfake faces contained different sets of attributes, and the registered valence-dominance structure was not fully replicated for the actual deepfake faces.

Furthermore, our Brunswikian lens model did not support H2a, yet provided preliminary insights into the utilization of social attributes during the detection task. Consistent with the initial hypothesis, trustworthiness did not significantly predict detection accuracy. However, contrary to expectations, attractiveness also failed to yield a significant effect. Whilst this finding contrasts with recent evidence using an identical stimulus set (Stockner et al., 2026), it underscores an important methodological insight. When evaluated in isolation, attractiveness often appears to predict detection accuracy (e.g., Miller et al., 2023; Tucciarelli et al., 2022) because it may regard (or act as a proxy for) other associated socio-cognitive traits. In a multi-attribute detection paradigm, like in the current study, however, this predictive power loses its relevance. This is highly consistent with the deception literature, in which single studies have, for instance, shown a wide series of cues to be associated with deception detection accuracy but the meta-analytic lens model by Hartwig and Bond (2011) found that only certain deception cues had diagnostic utility. Indeed, in real-life contexts, only a selected subset of dimensions may possess the necessary diagnostic utility to aid human detection. In this light, it is instead attributes considered less in the field of deepfake detection, such as weirdness, caringness, and intelligence, that may carry greater unique explanatory power.

Exploratory analyses based on H2b, which posited that specific traits may actively modulate performance, indicated both in the linear regression and the lens model a significant impact on detection performances. Given the high collinearity observed among these variables, we speculate that they are not strictly independent predictors, but rather as interdependent components of a broader heuristic system. On one hand, it is possible that weirdness may have operated as a cue for disrupting the observer's baseline "truth-default" state (e.g., Levine & Street, 2025), indirectly associated with enhanced detection accuracy of deepfake faces. In this regard, it is worth noting that we also encountered a negative direct effect of weirdness on overall detection accuracy, suggesting that underlying mechanisms, especially for real faces, might have also deceived human raters. On the other hand, caringness and intelligence may have triggered a positive "halo effect" (e.g., Beckwith & Lehmann, 1975). When a synthetic face is characterized by these traits, potentially fostering trust and suppressing the activation of suspicion (e.g., Oleszkiewicz et al., 2016), this may have led to higher perceived realness, with an associated decreasing deepfake detection accuracy. These findings also align closely with the findings of Maiano et al. (2024), who observed that general facial likeability similarly compromises deepfake identification performance. Crucially, sensitivity analysis excluding attributes with low reliability (i.e., intelligence, trustworthiness, emotional stability) showed non-significant effects of weirdness, but also converging evidence regarding caringness and its direct and indirect effects on detection accuracy. Thus, future research is needed to specifically disentangle the underlying cognitive mechanisms through which caringness ratings predict detection accuracy, as well as the predictive power of weirdness and intelligence, especially given the low reliability of the latter.

Relatedly, and finally, the lens model revealed that deepfake stimuli received higher ratings on a series of valence-related attributes (e.g., attractiveness, caringness, intelligence etc.) and lower ratings on meanness, weirdness, aggressiveness and unhappiness. This expands the existing literature showing that deepfake stimuli are more attractive (e.g., Miller et al., 2023). In fact, subjectively perceived deepfake attractiveness has been explained by research showing that AI-generated facial stimuli are more symmetric compared to real facial stimuli, both from an objective point of view (e.g., Boudnikova & Kleisner, 2024) and from a subjective point of view. Humans have rated AI-faces as more average (i.e., less distinctive) compared to real stimuli (e.g., Miller et al., 2023), i.e. attributes that have been widely associated with attractiveness ratings of faces (e.g., Jones et al., 2007). Our findings suggest that deepfakes are attributed overall to more positive traits compared to real faces.

Limitations, implications and future directions

The present study is not without limitations. First, significant task order effects were detected across experimental blocks. Nevertheless, given that the valence-dominance structure was successfully replicated for real faces, it is plausible that this order effect did not fundamentally compromise participants' attribute evaluations. Future studies should replicate our results in a between-subject design or adopt a multiple-session paradigm, possibly with a larger delay to mitigate such order effects of detection and rating tasks. Second, multicollinearity among specific lens model attributes precluded the definitive isolation of the independent statistical variance contributed by each individual trait in the entire set of attributes, and subsequent research, also adopting different statistical approaches could further disentangle the unique and shared variances of these social attributes in the context of deepfake detection. A related limitation regards the low reliability of ratings of trustworthiness, emotional stability, and intelligence for deepfake faces, which were excluded from the PCA but retained in the regression and lens model. While the latter step was in accordance with the preregistered Stage 1 analysis script, it was not explicitly stated in the Stage 1 manuscript. Therefore, sensitivity analysis on the remaining 10 attributes characterised by adequate reliability yielded more restricted findings, only supporting the impairing indirect effect of Stimulus type through caringness. Furthermore, to independently address block-averaging and task-order confounds, sensitivity analyses on first-block ratings yielded results convergent with our preregistered analyses, which, however, should be cautiously interpreted and their implications further investigated. Finally, as our deepfake stimulus set was associated with more positive attributes compared to real faces, future research should experimentally manipulate potential physical face characteristics associated with these ratings, in order to expand our results to more diverse stimuli sets.

Beyond these methodological constraints, the current findings present notable practical and ethical implications. The results underscore that deepfake detection extends beyond perceptual discrimination, also relying on subjective, socio-cognitive processing. Crucially, the observation that positive social cues, specifically perceived caringness and intelligence, can be associated with impaired detection accuracy for deepfake faces highlights a potential vulnerability, as deepfake faces with these characteristics tend to be perceived as real. In the current technological landscape, where Diffusion Models enable the highly realistic production of human faces via textual prompts, there is a substantial risk of adversarial applications such as identity theft, political misinformation and revenge porn (Farid, 2022). Therefore, the systematic investigation of factors impacting deepfake detection is crucial for the development of evidence-based training protocols and sensibility campaigns. Consequently, it is imperative for future research to integrate psychological science with digital ethics, considering the ethical use, investigation and dissemination of information in this field which should be safeguarded by public policies and democratic access to knowledge.

To conclude, our findings shed light, for the first time, into the cognitive processing of static deepfake faces and their social evaluation, whilst also providing preliminary insight into the potential underlying mechanisms associated with deepfake detection of highly standardized, frontal faces generated using diffusion-model technology.
